intro: Pickleball combines elements of tennis, badminton and table tennis on a small court with solid paddles and a perforated plastic ball. Two clever rules define it: the two-bounce rule slows down the start of every point, and the non-volley zone — 'the kitchen' — stops players smashing everything at the net. This entry follows the USA Pickleball rulebook, the most widely used reference.
inThirtySeconds: Serve underhand, diagonally, past the kitchen line.
The serve and the return must each bounce before they are hit (the two-bounce rule).
You can't volley while standing in the kitchen — the 7 ft zone next to the net.
Traditional games go to 11, win by 2, and only the serving side scores.
objective: Win rallies until you reach 11 points (or the format's target) with a two-point lead.

facts.players: 1 v 1 or 2 v 2 (doubles is most common)

scoring.label: Point
scoring.detail: In traditional side-out scoring, only the serving side can score.

scoring.label: Game
scoring.detail: Usually to 11, win by 2; tournaments may play to 15 or 21.

scoring.label: Score call
scoring.detail: In doubles: serving team's score, receiving team's score, and server number (1 or 2).

bodies.name: USA Pickleball
bodies.scope: US national governing body; publishes the Official Rulebook

rules.title: The underhand serve
rules.summary: The serve is hit with an upward, underhand motion, contacting the ball below the waist, and travels diagonally into the opposite service court.
rules.body: At least one foot must be behind the baseline, and the serve must clear the non-volley zone, including its line. A 'drop serve', where the ball is dropped and hit after it bounces, is also allowed under current rules. The server gets one attempt.

rules.title: Side-out scoring
rules.summary: Only the serving side scores points. In doubles both partners serve before the serve passes to the opponents.
rules.body: At the start of each game, only one player of the first serving team serves before a side-out, which is why the first score call is '0–0–2'. Some competitions use rally scoring instead, where every rally earns a point.
rules.example: Score called '5–3–1': the serving team has 5, the receivers have 3, and the first server is serving.

chapters.title: The two-bounce rule
chapters.summary: Why every point starts from the baseline.

rules.title: Let the first two shots bounce
rules.summary: The receiving team must let the serve bounce before returning it, and the serving team must let the return bounce before hitting it.
rules.body: After those two bounces, either side may volley or play off the bounce. The rule stops the serving team from rushing the net and makes points longer. Breaking it is a fault.
rules.example: The server's partner volleys the return of serve out of the air: fault, side-out or point to the receivers.

chapters.title: The kitchen
chapters.summary: The non-volley zone next to the net.

rules.title: No volleys in the non-volley zone
rules.summary: You may not volley the ball while touching the non-volley zone or its line.
rules.body: The restriction also applies to your momentum: if you volley outside the zone and your follow-through carries you into it — even after the ball is dead — it is a fault. You may enter the kitchen at any time to play a ball that has bounced.
rules.example: A player hits a volley with both feet behind the line, then stumbles and touches the kitchen line: fault.

rules.title: Dinking
rules.summary: Soft shots that drop into the opponent's kitchen ('dinks') are a core tactic.
rules.body: Because opponents can't volley a dink from inside the kitchen, they must let it bounce, which keeps rallies patient until someone hits a ball high enough to attack.

chapters.title: Faults
chapters.summary: Common ways to lose the rally.

rules.title: General faults
rules.summary: Hitting the ball out of bounds or into the net, a volley from the kitchen, or a two-bounce violation ends the rally.
rules.body: Lines are in, except the kitchen line on the serve, where touching it makes the serve a fault. Touching the net or posts with your body, paddle or clothing while the ball is in play is also a fault.

fouls.name: Kitchen violation
fouls.description: Volleying while touching the non-volley zone.

fouls.name: Two-bounce violation
fouls.description: Volleying the serve or the return of serve.

fouls.name: Short serve
fouls.description: Serve lands in the kitchen or on its line.

flow.title: Return and third shot
flow.description: Both must bounce; the third shot is often a soft 'drop' into the kitchen.

flow.title: At the net
flow.description: Players move up to the kitchen line and trade dinks and volleys.

flow.title: Side-out
flow.description: When the serving side loses rallies, the serve passes to the opponents.

positions.name: Server
positions.role: Starts each rally from behind the baseline.

positions.name: Partner at the kitchen line
positions.role: Moves forward to control the net once the return has bounced.

field.name: Court
field.dimensions: 20 ft × 44 ft (6.1 m × 13.4 m), for singles and doubles
notes: Non-volley zone: 7 ft on each side of the net
Net: 36 in at the sidelines, 34 in at the centre

glossary.definition: The non-volley zone next to the net.
A soft shot landing in the opponent's kitchen.
A soft shot after the return, used to reach the net safely.
Leaping around the kitchen post to volley from outside the court.

funFacts: Pickleball was invented in 1965 on Bainbridge Island, near Seattle, by three fathers improvising a game for their families.
Whether the name came from a 'pickle boat' crew or a family dog called Pickles is still debated.
